title: Andon board for a small assembly line: stations, alerts, response times
summary: One board that turns a call for help into a visible clock: six stations, three alert states, and response times everyone can see.

blocks.title: A problem at a station is a clock on the board
blocks.body: Andon is a simple deal: anyone on the line can call for help the moment something is wrong, and the call becomes public immediately - which station, what state, and how long it has been waiting. This board is a working example of that deal for a six-station line.

blocks.heading: The board, right now
blocks.caption: Amber means help requested, line still moving. Red means the station stopped - and the clock runs in the open.

items.label: Age of the red alert at Test - and counting, in front of everyone
Average response this week - target is under 2:00
Stations, each with a pull cord anyone can reach

blocks.heading: The three states and what they demand
items: Green - running. Nobody looks at green. That is the point of green.
Amber - help requested, station still working. A team lead responds; the line keeps moving while the problem is small.
Red - station stopped or about to stop the line. The response clock starts publicly. Red is not a reprimand; red is a flare.

items.title: Torque gun faults mid-cycle
items.detail: Operator pulls the cord. Station 3 goes amber on the board; the alert appears with its own clock.

items.title: Acknowledged
items.detail: Sam sees the board from the rework loop and taps the response button: someone is coming. The clock keeps running, now measuring travel.

items.title: Responder at the station
items.detail: Diagnosis starts. The line never stopped - this is what amber is for.

items.title: Cleared
items.detail: A dying battery pack, swapped. The alert closes and its full timeline lands in the log.

blocks.heading: Why the clock is the whole design
blocks.body: The board's power is not the colors - it is that response time is measured in public. A red alert aging past two minutes asks a question out loud. Teams that watch this number fall are watching help get faster; teams that hide it are watching the cord quietly stop being pulled. The metric is the culture.

blocks.title: The rule that keeps the cord being pulled
blocks.body: Alerts are for response, never for blame. The day someone is criticized for pulling the cord is the day the board starts lying - stations go quietly slow instead of honestly red. The board only tells the truth while pulling it is safe.

blocks.heading: Check the logic
blocks.prompt: Station 4 has been red for 2:40 with no responder assigned. What is the board's most useful next reader?
options: Whoever owns response assignment - the unassigned red is now their problem in public
The operator at station 4, to check whether they pulled the cord hard enough
Nobody - the board already recorded it for the weekly report
blocks.explanation: A red alert with no responder is a dispatch failure, and the board makes it impossible to miss. The cord already did its job; the response side of the deal is what is due now.
